entry.title: A Vaidya’s Library in Kathmandu
entry.content:
Madhu Bajra Bajracharya is an ayurvedic doctor who was trained by his father, the late Mana Bajra Bajracharya (d. 2001). They descend from a famous lineage of Buddhist priests, as Mana recounts in his autobiography:

By caste, we are Shakya related to the Shakya of Kapilavastu, the birthplace of Lord Gautama Buddha. During the medieval period, following the principles of Bajrayana, the third advanced stage of Buddhism (following Hinayana and Mahayana), our ancestors received the consecration of Bajrayana. This consecration bestows the title of Bajracharya. To have this title, one must follow the principles of the “Heruka Chaka Samvara Tantra.” Those with the title of Bajracharya are the priests of the Newari Buddhists, one of the ancient inhabitants of Kathmandu Valley.

In 1937, I received my formal initiation as a Bajracharya, which I needed to be a member of the Bihara. In 1944, I received my consecration as Bajrayana, which I needed to be an authorized Bajracharya. In 1945, I married with Gyani Devi Bajracharya. Marriage is essential for Bajrayana practice. We have a son and four daughters.

— Mana Bajra Bajracharya, “Introduction”

Vaidya Mana Bajra Bajracharya’s Ayurvedic teachings were the subject of the book first published in 2009 (Bajra Bajracharya, 2009). In 2015, one of the book’s editors, Alan Tilloton, wrote to Dominik Wujastyk, about the Bajra Bajracharya library of books and manuscripts, noting that the collection was of important cultural value and its future was uncertain.

The collection

According to Madhu Bajra Bajracharya, his father learnt Sanskrit and collected manuscripts of medical works. He became known locally as a collector and was consequently offered manuscripts on many other subjects. As a result, the current collection includes not only medical works but a wide variety of material ranging from grammar and philosophy to narrative, devotional and astrological texts.

Many years ago, Madhu Bajra Bajracharya compiled a handlist of the collection, which he kindly sent to Dominik Wujastyk in private correspondence. This handlist indicates that the collection contains many hundreds of manuscripts, at least forty-four of which are on medicine.

I visited Madhu Bajra Bajracharya’s house, where he kindly showed me the collection. It is kept in three large metal cabinets, with each manuscript wrapped in cloth and tied with string. Unfortunately, the manuscripts are currently piled up and jumbled together, so it is impossible to find any particular item without unpacking the cabinets. A handwritten handlist was made in 2014.

A palm-leaf Carakasaṃhitā

Fortunately, during my visit Madhu Bajra Bajracharya managed to find a palm-leaf manuscript of the Carakasaṃhitā, which is recorded as the first entry in the vaidyaśāstra section of his handlist. It is incomplete and undated, but judging from the condition of the palm leaves and the style of writing, it looked very old to me, possibly earlier than the fifteenth century. This manuscript left me with the impression that the collection likely holds some very old and valuable material.

Texts and experience

I had the opportunity to talk to Madhu Bajra Bajracharya about the future of the collection. He feels that his children are not particularly interested in it, and he himself no longer needs it, now that he has fifty years of experience as an ayurvedic doctor. He told me that texts are useful for those learning Ayurveda because they provide general information, but that the most valuable knowledge comes from practising Ayurveda, through which one learns how to diagnose and treat people according to their peculiarities. Doctors, he said, need to treat people rather than illnesses; experience provides knowledge of both, whereas texts are limited to the latter. His father tried to address this issue by recording notes in diaries about specific cases. Madhu Bajra Bajracharya showed me these diaries, which are written in Nepāl Bhāṣā, and said they are the only books on Ayurveda that he now consults.

The future of the collection

Although the manuscript collection has little practical value for him, Madhu Bajra Bajracharya recognises its importance for preserving the history and heritage of Nepal, and he would like the collection to be properly housed and cared for after his passing. To this end we discussed digitisation initiatives, such as the British Library’s Endangered Archives Programme. Digitisation may help to safeguard the contents, but one would hope that the manuscripts themselves eventually end up in the care of a professional library that can preserve them for future generations.

The handlist does not mention a manuscript of the Suśrutasaṃhitā, but Madhu Bajra Bajracharya believes there is one in his collection. We therefore hope to return next year, with more time in hand, to unpack the cabinets and search the collection more thoroughly.

entry.title: A Visit to the Sanjay Sharma Museum, Jaipur

link.title: A Visit to the Sanjay Sharma Museum, Jaipur

entry.content:
On Sunday, 11 October 2026, the two of us — Dominik Wujastyk and Jason Birch — made our first visit to the Shree Sanjay Sharma Museum and Research Institute in Jaipur. The museum stands on the Amer Road at Gujarghati, Parasrampuri, looking across the lake to the Jal Mahal. We came with two questions in mind: what manuscripts of the Suśrutasaṃhitā does the collection hold, and are there illustrated manuscripts on alchemy (rasaśāstra)?

The museum building on the Amer Road, opposite the Jal Mahal. (Image: Dominik Wujastyk and Jason Birch)

We were warmly received by Chaitanya Sharma, grandson of the museum’s founder, Ram Kṛpālu Sharma, who took us through the galleries. Chaitanya’s father, Shri Tilak Sharma, the Director of the Museum, joined us later and the following day.

A collection that began with four manuscripts

The museum’s origins are literary. In the 1950s Ram Kṛpālu Sharma, who began his career as a schoolteacher, struggled to get his own writings published: a book of prose and verse, Prāñjali, appeared only after great difficulty, and a second, Vāṅmayī, never saw print for lack of funds. That experience led him, from 1955, to start collecting and preserving manuscripts — beginning with just four. The collection was first known as the Sharma Grantha Saṅgrahālaya. After the untimely death of his younger son, and Tilak’s brother, Sanjay Sharma, in 1982, it took its present name. With his wife Padmavati Sharma and the wider family, the founder went on to build the museum and library collections, and the institution remains a private, family-run foundation.

The family now describes the collection as numbering around a hundred thousand manuscripts, together with artefacts that illustrate their subjects. According to the Museums of India listing, the holdings span more than 200 subjects in some 16 languages and scripts — among them Brāhmī, Śāradā, Tibetan, Arabic, Persian, Tirhutā, Bengali, Telugu, Gujarati, Oriya, Gurmukhi and Devanāgarī — on palm leaf, birch bark and paper. Subject areas named include Vedic literature, jyotiṣa, tantra, dhanurveda, āyurveda and medicine, and “alchemy and chemistry”.

Manuscript cabinets in the library. (Image: Sanjay Sharma Museum.)

The galleries

One of the painting galleries, with porcelain and a silver swing (hiṇḍolā) in the central case. (Image: Sanjay Sharma Museum.)

We were stunned by the extent and quality of the manuscripts, paintings and artifacts on display in the museum’s numerous spacious and marble-tiled galleries. Any visitor to Jaipur with an interest in Indian history and culture must not leave without a visit to this extraordinary collection.

The museum is laid out in several galleries: glass painting and porcelain; miniature painting (fifteenth to nineteenth centuries, from Jaipur, Kishangarh, Kota, Bundi, Bikaner, Nathdwara and elsewhere); textiles and costumes, largely from the Jaipur court; cloth paintings and picchvāīs; an art gallery; illustrated manuscripts; and the manuscript library itself.

The long gallery of large cloth paintings. (Image: Sanjay Sharma Museum.)

A Devanāgarī manuscript from Jaipur, dated 1588 CE. (Image: Museums of India.)

Among the illustrated material is a late nineteenth-century cosmological painting from Jaipur depicting the fourteen worlds (caturdaśabhuvana), from a series catalogued as the Viśvavijñāna-citrāvalī (1895). The tantra holdings include yantras such as an eighteenth-century Śani-yantra from Marwar.

In the Museum, photography is strictly prohibited, so we are unfortunately unable to illustrate any of the following remarks.

What we were looking for

The Suśrutasaṃhitā

As the Suśruta Project website explains, our project is focused on the textual and doctrinal differences between The Compendium as it existed in the earliest manuscript of 878 CE and the later “vulgate” version that was edited and reshaped by medieval commentators over the centuries. Manuscripts matter to the project, helping us to understand the history of this foundational work of medicine. We are trying to include as many manuscripts as possible in our research.

During our visit on 11 and 12 October, we saw a Suśrutasaṃhitā manuscript on display, but unfortunately we were not permitted to examine it. It is numbered MS Jaipur Sanjay Sharma Museum RN4MSS 4720. The single leaf on display had text that appeared to be a commentary on the main work, in a section about the Ayurvedic concept of “appropriateness” (Skt. sātmya). One passage cited the author Caraka. On the second day of our visit, Shri Tilak Sharma, the Museum’s Director, shared with us a photocopy of the last two folios of the manuscript. They showed it to be the ending of the last chapter of the Uttaratantra, with the final “Candraṭa” verse that we have discussed in another blog. We hope the Museum will see a way to share a digital image of the whole MS with us in due course.

Illustrated rasaśāstra

Professor Dagmar Wujastyk has been researching the history of Indian alchemy for several years. She has published several research articles on the history of rasaśāstra and on illustrated rasaśāstra manuscripts (Wujastyk, 2024). Her most recent book on the history of Indian alchemy was published by Oxford University Press in 2025 (Wujastyk, 2025). Professor Wujastyk had asked me to look out for illustrated alchemical manuscripts and I was delighted to see a richly illustrated copy of an unnamed alchemical rasaśāstra text in bhāṣā in one of the display cabinets. However, photography was not allowed and for the time being, since manuscripts are not being made available for study, research has to stop there.

Next steps

This was not my first visit to the Museum. In 2011, while working on the Vienna project on the Carakasaṃhitā, I visited the Museum in its former premises inside the Pink City. I went there to buy Ram Kṛpālu Sharma’s catalogue of the Museum’s Hindi manuscripts, a fine book with good illustrations. Shri Tilak Sharma kindly showed me some of the rooms that were then being reorganised, among them a room with fifteen to twenty almirahs (cupboards) full of manuscripts, two of them holding palm-leaf manuscripts alone. The collection was in the middle of a move, and there was as yet no way of searching it systematically. When I asked about manuscripts of the Carakasaṃhitā, I was assured that a collection of this size, one of the largest in India, would certainly contain them: Shri Ram Kṛpālu Sharma recalled one complete copy and several partial ones, probably of the eighteenth or nineteenth century. We parted on warm terms, having even discussed the idea of preparing, with Ram Kṛpālu Sharma and perhaps David White, a catalogue of the Museum’s richly illustrated rasaśāstra manuscripts. The Caraka Project came to an end some years ago and funding ended for the project, so the chance to collaborate with the Sanjay Sharma Museum remained unfulfilled.

Director Tilak Sharma said that there was no handlist of the 125,000 manuscripts in the collection, so it is difficult to know whether there are more copies of the Suśrutasaṃhitā, Rasaratnākara, or other interesting works in the collection. As in 2011, it seems very likely that the library holds a substantial body of Āyurvedic manuscripts, including copies of the Carakasaṃhitā and other classic works.

The Museum is negotiating with Gyan Bharatam, and it is to be hoped that a mutually beneficial MOU can be signed in the future that will help the library collection become accessible to research scholars.

Visiting

The museum is open daily from 9:00 am to 5:30 pm; allow one to two hours. Photography is not permitted inside. Contact details are on the museum’s website.

entry.title: A Visit to the Āmer Śāstra Bhaṇḍār, Jaipur

link.title: A Visit to the Āmer Śāstra Bhaṇḍār, Jaipur

entry.content:
On 12 October 2026, Jason Birch and I visited the Āmer Śāstra Bhaṇḍār in Jaipur, a Digambara Jain manuscript library. Our aim was to see a manuscript of the Suśrutasaṃhitā that had been recorded there in the mid-twentieth century.

The library

The Āmer Śāstra Bhaṇḍār has been housed in several places in Rajasthan over its history. It was formerly known as the Bhaṭṭāraka Devendrakīrti Bhaṇḍār and was originally kept in the Digambara Jain temple of Neminātha at Amber. It was later moved to the Mahāvīra Jaina Bhavana in Jaipur, and then to Śrī Mahāvīrjī.

Today the collection is hosted by the Apabhraṃśa Sāhitya Akādamī evaṃ Pustakālaya (the Apabhraṃśa Literary Academy and Library), an institution of the Digambar Jain Atishay Kshetra Shri Mahaviraji dedicated to teaching Apabhraṃśa, the language of many Jain literary and religious works. The address is Block B, Malviya Nagar, Jaipur, Rajasthan 302017, not far from Jaipur’s airport.

Catalogues and studies

The library was catalogued by Kastūrcanda Kāslīvāl in 1949, in the first volume of his Rājasthān ke Jaina Śāstra Bhaṇḍārom kī grantha sūcī (Biswas, no. 0891, vol. 1):

A year later Kāslīvāl published a companion volume, the Praśasti Saṅgraha, collecting the colophons (praśasti) of manuscripts in the same collection (Biswas, no. 0427):

Important contemporary information on the library, its contents and its history is given by Ulrich Timme Kragh:

  • Kragh, Ulrich Timme (2013), ‘Localized Literary History: Sub-Text and Cultural Heritage in the Āmer Śāstrabhaṇḍār, a Digambara Manuscript Repository in Jaipur’, International Journal of Jaina Studies 9/3: 1–53.
  • Kragh, Ulrich Timme, and Abhishek Jain (2019), ‘A Preliminary Study on the Indian Grammar Manuscripts of the Āmer Śāstrabhaṇḍār in Jaipur’, Przegląd Orientalistyczny 2019/1: 3–21.

The Suśrutasaṃhitā manuscript

Kāslīvāl’s list (p. 154) records a single manuscript of the Suśrutasaṃhitā, containing only the Kalpasthāna, in 21 folios:

The entry reads:

भाषा-संस्कृत। पत्र संख्या २१. साइज १०॥×४॥ इञ्च। लिपि संवत् १७०२. केवल कल्पस्थान ही है।

That is: language Sanskrit; 21 folios; size 10½ × 4½ inches; copied in Saṃvat 1702 (1645/46 CE); contains only the Kalpasthāna.

Our visit

At the library we met the Director, Smt. Shakuntala Jain, who received us kindly.

Unfortunately, the manuscript recorded in Kāslīvāl’s catalogue is no longer in the collection. Smt. Jain produced a handwritten list of the Āyurvedic titles held in the library, and the Suśrutasaṃhitā was not among them. We were not able to photograph the list. It seems, sadly, that MS Jaipur Āmer Śāstra Bhaṇḍār Kāslīvāl 154 was lost at some time between 1950 and 2026.

We thank Smt. Shakuntala Jain for her welcome and for her help in searching the collection.

entry.title: Candraṭa’s editing of the Suśrutasaṃhitā, updated October 2026

link.title: Candraṭa’s editing of the Suśrutasaṃhitā, updated October 2026

entry.content:
Update of 2026: new example from the Sanjay Sharma Museum, Jaipur

To the original blog post (below), we can now add the colophon of MS Jaipur Sanjay Sharma Museum RN4MSS 4720:

sauśrute caṃdraṭeneha bhiṣakṭīsaṭasūnunā pāṭhaśuddhiḥ kṛtā taṃtro | ṭīkām ālokya jaijjaṭīṃ| iti sauśrute āyurvedaśāstre uttarasthānaṃ samāptaṃ // 1 // saṃ 1688 varṣe nabhasi mā

The reading “tantro” for “tantre” is probably the scribe’s mistaken inclusion of the following daṇḍa in the syllable: तन्त्रे॥ -> तन्त्रो।

Original post of September 2024

Candraṭa was a Sanskrit author on medical topics who lived in the period 900-1050 CE (Meulenbeld, 1999, pp. IIA: 122–125). He is perhaps best known for writing a commentary on his father Tīsaṭa’s treatise, Cikitsākalikā. But Candraṭa wrote several other works, and of most relevance to our project is his “Editorial Corrections to the Suśruta text” (Suśrutapāṭhaśuddhi). Candraṭa himself said that he created this work, in a verse included at the end of his commentary on the Cikitsākalikā:

cikitsākalikāṭīkāṃ yogaratnasamuccayam/
suśrute pāṭhaśuddhiṃ ca tritayaṃ candraṭo vyadhat//

“I created the following three works: the commentary on the Cikitsākalikā, the Yogaratnasamuccaya and the Suśrutapāṭhaśuddhi (`Correction of the Text of the Suśruta’).”

— MS Oxford Bodleian Library Fraser 21 (Aufrecht, 1864, pp. 358, entry no. 852), dated 1530 CE.

An authorial statement is also found in some colophons of the Suśrutapāṭhaśuddhi itself, as is shown on f. 59 of MS London IOLR Taylor 1842 (Eggeling catalogue no. 2646):

[corrected transcription:] > sauśrute caṃdraṭeneha bhiṣakṭīsaṭasūnunā /
pāṭhaśuddhiḥ kṛtā taṃtre ṭīkām ālokya jaijjaṭīṃ //

“The correction of readings (pāṭhaśuddhi) in the treatise of Suśruta was done by Candraṭa the son of the doctor Tīsaṭa, after studying the commentary of Jejjaṭa.”

Another MS that has the same statement is MS Bikaner Anup 4391 (Kunhan Raja Catalogue p. 337):

In an undated manuscript of the Suśrutasaṃhitā, śārīrasthāna, from Kurukṣetra, we find the same text in a section colophon, but in a slightly expanded form (MS Kurukṣetra Jawaharlal Nehru Library 19786, f. 78v):

sūtrasthānaṃ nidānena śārīreṇa samanvitaṃ /
samāptaṃ vai turīyaṃ te vakṣyāmy atra cikitsitaṃ //
sauśrute caṃdraṭeneha bhiṣakṭīsaṭasūnunā /
pāṭhaśuddhiḥ kṛtā taṃtre ṭīkām ālokya jaijjaṭīṃ // ḥ // śrīḥ//

“The sūtrasthāna has been completed, with the nidāna and śārīra sthānas, and I will explain the fourth, the cikitsāsthāna. The Correction of Readings (pāṭhaśuddhi) in the treatise of Suśruta was done by Candraṭa the son of the doctor Tīsaṭa, after studying the commentary of Jejjaṭa.”

The Kurukṣetra colophon above has the extra initial statement, “I will explain (vakṣyāmi).” It is not clear whose voice this is. Is it the scribe? But vakṣyāmi is normally an authorial expression, where a scribe would be more likely to say something like likhyate mayā. The second statement, which is the same as that of the London MS, is more straightforward: Candraṭa wrote The Correction of Readings. This sounds like a statement by Candraṭa himself. However, this raises the question of why the statement appears at the end of the Kurukṣetra manuscript, which contains only the Suśrutasaṃhitā, and does not include Candraṭa’s work. However, it is definitely of interest that the scribe of the Kurukṣetra manuscript was aware of Candraṭa’s work and thought of it as a relevant reference to raise in the context of a manuscript of the Suśrutasaṃhitā. This means that several centuries after Candraṭa, the Suśrutasaṃhitā was thought of as a work that he had corrected.

entry.title: A Visit to the Kaiser Library, Kathmandu

link.title: A Visit to the Kaiser Library, Kathmandu

entry.content:
On 30 September 2026 we visited the Kaiser Library in Kathmandu. The library is the home of MS Kathmandu KL 699, the palm-leaf manuscript of the Suśrutasaṃhitā copied in 878 CE, which has been at the centre of the Suśruta Project’s work since its first phase. The purpose of the visit was to meet the library’s staff, to see the manuscript, and to propose a collaboration on its publication.

The Kaiser Library

The library was founded in 1907 by the Rana prime minister Chandra Shumsher for his son, Kaiser Shumsher Rana, who built it into one of the great private collections of South Asia. After Kaiser Shumsher’s death the library passed to the Government of Nepal, and it opened to the public in 1969. It is housed in the Kaiser Mahal palace complex on Kantipath, in the centre of Kathmandu. Alongside some 50,000 printed books, it holds an important collection of manuscripts on palm leaf and paper (see Dimitrov and Tamot 2007). KL 699 is the most celebrated of these, and is listed in UNESCO’s Memory of the World Asia-Pacific Register.

Our hosts

We were received by the Chief Librarian, Mr Pradip Bhattarai, and by Ms Binita Giri of the library staff. Both were cordial and welcoming, and generous with their time. We also had the pleasure of meeting Ambika Prasad Regmi, who is preparing a Nepali translation of the Suśrutasaṃhitā based on KL 699. It is very good to know that the manuscript’s text is being made available to readers in Nepal in their own language.

We were accompanied and introduced by Prof. Diwakar Acharya, Spalding Professor of Eastern Religions and Ethics at the University of Oxford. His help in making introductions and in explaining our goals in Nepali was invaluable, and we are most grateful to him.

Seeing KL 699

At our request, the manuscript was fetched from the stack and carefully unwrapped and laid out for us on the Chief Librarian’s table. It is a beautiful object. The scribe wrote in small, neat letters, evenly spaced across the long palm leaves, and the text is a pleasure to read.

The leaves are now somewhat dry and fragile, however, and we discussed with Mr Bhattarai the importance of handling the manuscript as little as possible. This is one of the strongest arguments for a good photographic record: once high-quality images are published, scholars will rarely need to consult the original leaves at all.

MS Kathmandu KL 699 unwrapped on the Chief Librarian's table at the Kaiser Library, 30 September 2026.

The library also keeps a register of the manuscripts photographed under its Kaiser Library Manuscript Collection Project, recording for each item its accession number, the corresponding NGMPP microfilm reel, title, subject, extent, size, script and condition.

A proposed facsimile edition

We proposed to the Chief Librarian that the Kaiser Library and the Suśruta Project collaborate on a facsimile edition of MS Kathmandu KL 699. The facsimile would be accompanied by a diplomatic transcription of the text, building on the transcription prepared during the first phase of the project. Such an edition would make this unique witness to the early history of Indian medicine available to scholars everywhere, while protecting the original from further handling.

Mr Bhattarai responded positively to the proposal. He will pass the plan to the library’s legal office and to the Ministry of Education for approval. We look forward to hearing from him and, we hope, to beginning work together.

We thank Mr Pradip Bhattarai, Ms Binita Giri and Ambika Prasad Regmi for their warm welcome, and Prof. Diwakar Acharya for making the meeting possible.

entry.title: Nirāmayatā: Healing and Wellbeing at the India International Centre, New Delhi

link.title: Nirāmayatā: Healing and Wellbeing at the India International Centre, New Delhi

entry.content:
On 6–7 October 2026, three members of the Suśruta Project, Dominik Wujastyk, Jason Birch and Kenneth Zysk, took part in the international conference Nirāmayatā (निरामयता): Healing and Wellbeing in South Asian Texts and Practices, held at the India International Centre (IIC) in New Delhi. We were the guests of the IIC–International Research Division (IRD) and its Executive Director, Dr Sudha Gopalakrishnan, who conceived the conference and invited us to speak.

The IRD and the SAMHiTA programme

The International Research Division grew out of the IIC-Asia Project, which from 1997 onward held annual conferences on the cultures of Asia, for many years under the guidance of Dr Kapila Vatsyayan. Since 2022 the Division has run SAMHiTA (South Asian Manuscript Histories and Textual Archive), a programme supported by the Ministry of External Affairs to inventory, catalogue and digitise South Asian manuscripts held in libraries and archives outside India. Its knowledge partners include the PANDiT project, the Old Indian Institute at Oxford, SOAS, the Wellcome Collection, the Royal Danish Library and the Bibliothèque nationale de France.

The Nirāmayatā conference was organised by the IRD in collaboration with the Indian Council for Cultural Relations and the Bharat ki Soch Foundation, within the framework of SAMHiTA. Its aim was to look at Indian and wider Asian medical traditions through manuscripts and living practice: how medical knowledge was produced, circulated and transformed, and how it moved between Sanskrit, Tamil, Persianate, Tibetan and Southeast Asian traditions. Over two days, six sessions brought together historians, philologists, practitioners of Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani and Sowa Rigpa, and biomedical scientists.

Our presentations

Keynote address. After the inaugural addresses by Shri K. N. Shrivastava (Director, IIC), Dr Sudha Gopalakrishnan, Shri Anil Rajput (Bharat ki Soch) and Shri Shyam Saran (President, IIC), Dominik Wujastyk gave the keynote address, “Achieving Healthiness and the Absence of Illness in Ayurveda.” The title takes up the theme of the conference itself, since nirāmayatā means “freedom from disease.”

Dissection in the Suśrutasaṃhitā. In the first session, “Texts and Concepts on Medical Thought,” chaired by Prof. G. G. Gangadharan, Kenneth Zysk spoke on “What Medical Literature Can Reveal: Dissection in the Suśruta Saṃhitā, Internal and External Transmission.” The Suśrutasaṃhitā’s instructions for preparing and examining a human body in the Śārīrasthāna are unique in early Indian literature, and raise questions both about how this knowledge was passed on within the medical tradition and about its relations with knowledge from outside it.

Suśruta on preserving health. In the afternoon session, “Mind and Body in Asian Medical Traditions,” chaired by Dr S. Irfan Habib, Jason Birch spoke on “From Svastharakṣaṇīya to Svasthavṛtti: How Suśruta’s Chapter on Preserving a Person’s Health Changed.” The paper traced how the Suśrutasaṃhitā’s teaching on keeping a healthy person healthy was reshaped over the course of the work’s transmission.

Other contributions

Our papers sat alongside a wide range of others (program). Among them were Dr S. A. S. Sarma on Gāruḍa Tantra traditions of snakebite medicine in Kerala; Dr Mehsaan Barawaz on the Persian Majmūʿah-i Żiyāʾī and the meeting of Unani and Ayurvedic learning; Dr Padma Gurmet on Sowa Rigpa; Sugi Lanus on herbal and ritual healing in Balinese lontar manuscripts; Dr Annamma Spudich on European documents about South Indian medicine in the sixteenth to eighteenth centuries; and Prof. Nupur Dasgupta on regional environmental knowledge in Cakrapāṇidatta’s Dravyaguṇasaṃgraha and Mādhavakara’s Paryāyaratnamālā. A session on traditional and modern medicine, with Prof. Bhushan Patwardhan and Prof. Rama Jayasundar, and a closing round table on future directions for traditional knowledge, chaired by Vaidya Rajesh Kotecha, brought the perspectives of science and public policy into the discussion.

Thanks

We are very grateful to Dr Sudha Gopalakrishnan and the staff of the International Research Division for their invitation, their careful organisation and their generous hospitality. The day after the conference, on 8 October, we also visited the Ministry of Culture and Gyan Bharatam, the national manuscript mission; that visit is described in a separate post.

entry.title: Visiting the Āśā Saphū Kuthi, Kathmandu

link.title: Visiting the Āśā Saphū Kuthi, Kathmandu

entry.content:
In early October 2026 I visited the Āśā Saphū Kuthi in Kathmandu, a library best known for its Nepāl Bhāṣā (Newar) books and manuscripts, to look for manuscripts of the Suśrutasaṃhitā.

Finding the library

It is impossible to see the library building from the main road (Cittadhar Mārg), which is lined with two-storey shopfronts. Between two of the shops, a doorway with a carved wooden architrave opens onto a corridor that leads to a courtyard behind them. High above the doorway, and hard to see from street level, a sign in Rañjanā script reads Āśā Saphūkuthi.

As one emerges from the corridor, a three-storeyed library building in traditional Newar style towers above. Over the porch the name is set in gilt letters in the same script, with “The Āśā Archives” in English beside it.

A morning with the catalogue

The library opens at 11 am. The front door is not locked but needs a good push; not knowing this, I waited outside until someone who did arrived. In the morning the library is staffed by an assistant, who showed me the printed catalogue of manuscripts (Śākya, 2000). It is arranged by subject, so I went straight to the medical (vaidya) section.

The collection of medical works is fairly impressive. The section has nearly two hundred entries, many of them works in Nepāl Bhāṣā or bilingual Sanskrit–Nepāl Bhāṣā texts on diseases, diagnosis, pulse, remedies and mantras.

Viewing the scans

The librarian does not arrive until after 3 pm, so my visit was punctuated by a long lunch at a nearby restaurant. I got the impression that the whole manuscript collection has been digitised and is stored on hard drives kept in a locked cabinet. The librarian, who holds the key, did indeed arrive at 3 pm. She was very friendly and let me look at whatever manuscript scans I wanted, at a fee of 100 NPR an hour on the library’s computer.

What I found

Among the Sanskrit medical works, two stand out: a complete manuscript of the relatively rare Mādhavacikitsā (DPN 1599), and an incomplete one of Ravigupta’s Siddhasāra (DPN 1660, chapters 1–8). There is also a damaged fragment of an illustrated work on horse medicine (aśvacikitsā) with four hand-painted illustrations of horses. A second veterinary text, a Śālihotra in Sanskrit and Maithilī, is also listed in the catalogue.

Unfortunately for us, there were no Suśrutasaṃhitā manuscripts.

Practical notes for visitors

  • The library opens at 11 am every day except Saturday. Push the front door firmly.
  • The librarian, who controls access to the scans, arrives after 3 pm.
  • Viewing scans costs 100 NPR an hour.
  • There is a photocopier. Digital images of manuscripts may perhaps be purchased, but I did not broach that topic.

For anyone working on Sanskrit or Newar medicine, the Āśā Saphū Kuthi repays the afternoon’s wait.

Background: the library and its collection

The Āśā Saphū Kuthi (आशा सफू कुथि, “Āśā’s book house”), also called the Āśā Archives, is a free public library across Cittadhar Mārg from the Raktakālī temple. As Rhishav Sapkota describes (Sapkota, 2021), it is named after Āśā Mān Siṃh Kansakar (1916–1990), founder of the Nepāl Bhāṣā publisher Cwāsā Pāsā, who resolved that Nepal should keep its own manuscripts rather than see them sold abroad. His son, the politician Prem Bahadur Kansakar, carried the project forward, and the American scholar Ian Alsop gave almost 500 manuscripts. The present building, funded by the Toyota Foundation, opened on 7 December 1987.

The early collection holds over 7,000 manuscripts from the fifteenth to the nineteenth century, in Sanskrit, Nepāl Bhāṣā and Nepali, on religion, poetics, astronomy, astrology and medicine. The catalogue I used, Āśā Saphūkuthiyā Saphū Dhalaḥ: A Short Catalogue of Āśā Archives, was compiled by Rājā Śākya and published in N.S. 1120 (2000 CE) (Śākya, 2000); each entry gives a DPN number, script, language, date, size, folios and material. An earlier catalogue of the library’s inscriptions and documents appeared in 1991 (Vaidya & Kansakar, 1991).

The scans I saw are the fruit of several digitization projects: a first phase led by Shucho Takaoka in 1987; the University of Hamburg’s Preserving the Written Heritage of Nepal (2018–2022); and the Hill Museum & Manuscript Library’s digitization of 1,332 items from the “new collection” (2019–2024, DPN 07172–08121). Many manuscript scans are now available through the Āśā Archives page at Archive.org.

entry.title: A Visit to Gyan Bharatam and the Ministry of Culture, New Delhi

link.title: A Visit to Gyan Bharatam and the Ministry of Culture, New Delhi

entry.content:
On 8 October 2026, three members of the Suśruta Project, Dominik Wujastyk, Jason Birch and Kenneth Zysk, spent an afternoon in New Delhi as guests of Gyan Bharatam, the Government of India’s national mission for the survey, conservation and digitisation of manuscripts.

Gyan Bharatam (Jñānabhāratam) was announced in the Union Budget for 2025–26 as a flagship programme of the Ministry of Culture. It builds on the work of the National Mission for Manuscripts, founded in 2003, and aims to document, conserve and make available more than ten million manuscripts held in libraries, institutions and private collections across India. The mission’s emblem carries the motto na hi jñānena sadṛśaṃ pavitram iha vidyate, “for nothing in this world purifies like knowledge” (Bhagavadgītā 4.38ab).

Meeting with the Secretary of the Ministry of Culture

Gyan Bharatam’s director, Dr Anirban Dash, first took us to the Ministry of Culture at Kartavya Bhavan. There we had an hour-long meeting with Shri Vivek Agarwal, Secretary of the Ministry of Culture, who has overall charge of the Gyan Bharatam mission.

The Secretary outlined the ambitious goals of the Government of India’s drive to digitise manuscripts across the country. He then listened carefully to our ideas and suggestions, drawn from our experience of working with Sanskrit medical manuscripts in Indian and international collections. He generously offered the support of Gyan Bharatam for projects that we might propose for action. We are very grateful for his time and his openness to collaboration.

Round table at Gyan Bharatam: “The Future of Manuscript Research”

After the meeting with the Secretary, we moved to the offices of Gyan Bharatam for an hour-long consultative round table on “The Future of Manuscript Research.” The session was chaired by Dr Anirban Dash, with members of the Gyan Bharatam team, and was live-streamed online.

The discussion ranged over the goals and meaning of Gyan Bharatam’s work and the importance and value of manuscript studies. Manuscripts are the primary evidence for almost everything we know about India’s intellectual history, including its medicine. The texts we read in printed editions are reconstructions from these witnesses, and their quality depends on the range and accuracy of the manuscripts consulted. A national effort to locate, catalogue and digitise manuscripts therefore directly benefits work such as ours on the Suśrutasaṃhitā and its commentaries. The session closed with questions from participants both in the room and online.

At Gyan Bharatam we were welcomed in the traditional manner with shawls and gifts of books.

We thank Dr Anirban Dash and the Gyan Bharatam team for their warm hospitality and for organising both meetings, and Shri Vivek Agarwal for his interest and encouragement. We look forward to developing proposals for collaboration in the coming months.

entry.title: A New Manuscript of Gayadāsa’s Nyāyacandrikā

link.title: A New Manuscript of Gayadāsa’s Nyāyacandrikā

entry.content:
Dr Harshal Bhatt, a long-term research associate of the Suśruta Project, recently conducted a research trip to Jaipur, where he obtained a digital copy of manuscript RORI 6838. Our team has only begun to examine this source, but it already appears exciting for two reasons. First, it preserves a substantial copy of Gayadāsa’s Nyāyacandrikā, extending from Sūtrasthāna 18 to the end of the Śārīrasthāna. Preliminary comparison suggests that its text is considerably better than that of the witnesses previously available for these sections. Second, it also transmits the mūla of the Suśrutasaṃhitā, with readings that differ from the vulgate, whose text appears largely to reflect the readings preferred by Ḍalhaṇa.

The significance of these textual features will become clearer as our work progresses. This post is limited to the manuscript as a physical and historical artifact: its extent, foliation, layout, state of preservation, and scribal colophons. It does not assess the text transmitted by the manuscript. That subject will be addressed separately once we have examined it more fully.

Contents and physical description

Contents, foliation, and sequence

The manuscript is incomplete and partly damaged, as discussed below. Its extant portion begins with Gayadāsa’s commentary on the opening of Sūtrasthāna 18 and continues to the end of the Śārīrasthāna, covering Sūtrasthāna 18–46, Nidānasthāna 1–16, and Śārīrasthāna 1–10.

The RORI catalogue lists the manuscript under serial number 3988. It gives the folio size as 30 × 13 cm and records a total of 774 folios. It states that folios 4–215 are missing, folio 287 occurs twice, and folios 656–665 are unnumbered. (Vinayasagar & Baldwa, 1948, pp. 444–445)

The digital copy allows us to refine this description:

  1. The manuscript did extend to folio 774. Although the foliation is lost from the final folio, the preceding folio is numbered 773.
  2. As far as we can tell, the entire opening section, folios 1–215, is now missing.
  3. Folios 656–665 were probably numbered originally. Their right margins, where the folio numbers would have appeared, have broken away.
  4. Two consecutive folios are numbered 287. A second hand, possibly that of a cataloguer, has distinguished them as prathama and dvi. Both are in the correct order and transmit a continuous passage of Gayadāsa’s commentary on Sūtrasthāna 26.9–10.

The foliation from 216 to 774 accounts for 559 numbered folios. Since folio number 287 occurs twice, the physical bundle should contain 560 folios, or 1,120 folio sides. The digital copy, however, contains only 1,115 photographs of individual sides. This difference does not necessarily indicate that any complete folios are missing.

The physical bundle appears to be largely arranged in textual order, and the digital copy seems to reproduce this arrangement faithfully. The clear exception is a group of five photographed sides placed at the front of the bundle. These apparently represent three displaced folios: one contains the end of the Nidānasthāna and its final colophon, while the other two contain the beginning of the Śārīrasthāna. Their foliation is no longer preserved, and we therefore cannot assign them folio numbers with confidence.

Several unphotographed sides can be identified at transitions between sections. The side preceding the colophon to the Sūtrasthāna is numbered 562v, so the colophon must stand on 563r. Since the Nidānasthāna begins on 564v, 563v and 564r were not photographed. At the next transition, the colophon to the Nidānasthāna appears on a verso, and the Śārīrasthāna begins on the verso of the following folio. The intervening recto is absent from the group of photographs placed at the front of the bundle. These sides were probably blank or nearly blank, although the rectos may have contained section titles.

Together with the presumably blank verso of the final folio, this accounts for four of the five unphotographed sides implied by the photograph count. The location of the remaining side cannot yet be determined, but it probably represents another blank or nearly blank side omitted by the photographer. The photograph count therefore gives no reason to suppose that a complete folio is missing.

Layout, decoration, and scribal practices

The manuscript is written in a clear variety of Devanagari. Each side contains ten lines, with approximately 40–45 akṣaras per line.

Most physical damage is confined to the margins and does not affect the text. The main exception is a large wormhole on the right side of folios 426–547. Its size varies, but at its largest it crosses seven lines and is approximately seven or eight akṣaras wide.

Straight orange-red lines mark the left and right edges of the writing area. Each verso also has an orange circle in both margins, occasionally expanded into a floral design. We have not yet identified a pattern governing the use of the more elaborate form.

The main foliation appears in the lower part of the right margin on each verso. The Nidānasthāna and Śārīrasthāna also have separate sectional foliations, each beginning with 1, at the bottom of the same margin. The right margins of the final Nidānasthāna folios are broken away, but the section appears to extend over approximately 100 folios. The Śārīrasthāna occupies 111 folios.

The manuscript is extensively rubricated in orange-red ink, although the purpose of every instance of rubrication is not yet clear. Identifiable examples include colophons, phrases introducing citations, and a red cha marking the beginning of a passage from the mūla.

Scribal colophons

In addition to the colophons marking the ends of individual chapters and sthānas, the manuscript preserves three longer scribal colophons: one each at the ends of the Sūtrasthāna, Nidānasthāna, and Śārīrasthāna. They provide valuable historical evidence about the manuscript’s production. I first present the three transcriptions with photographs and then discuss them together.

In the transcriptions, strikethrough reproduces text deleted by the scribe. Curly brackets { } enclose text removed by editorial emendation, while angle brackets ⟨ ⟩ contain editorial additions, replacements, or restorations. Thus, a replacement is written as {original}⟨emendation⟩. Superscript and subscript reproduce additions written above or below the line. A red dotted underline marks an uncertain reading, while a wavy underline marks a problematic form retained as written. Hyphens have been added editorially to mark boundaries within compounds and make the text easier to read.

Scribal colophon at the end of the Sūtrasthāna

The right-hand margin has broken away, and part of the text is lost. Missing passages have been supplied from the parallel formulations in the other two colophons.

Reading the colophons

All three colophons contain substantially the same information. Their Sanskrit is compressed and often syntactically irregular, but their general meaning remains clear. As Nalini Balbir has shown in her study of Western Indian manuscript colophons (Balbir & Ciotti, 2022), these texts commonly follow a conventional sequence of elements even when their grammatical relationships are only loosely expressed. The colophons of RORI 6838 correspond closely to this pattern: they record the extent of the text, the date and place of copying, the reigning ruler, the commissioner and his family, the intended purpose of the copy, the scribe, and concluding benedictions or scribal formulas.

The following sense-based translation draws primarily on the fullest wording preserved at the end of the Sūtrasthāna. It smooths out the syntax and does not attempt to resolve every problematic reading.

The extent of the text is 13,800 granthas. In Vikrama Saṃvat 1525, on the seventh tithi of the bright half of Bhādrapada, a Sunday—today, here in the city of Ahmedabad, during the victorious reign of Sultan Śrī Maḥmūd—Minister Śrī Māṇḍaṇa, son of the eminent physician and minister Śrī Nārāyaṇa and a member of the Ābhyantara Nāgara community, caused Gayadāsa’s commentary on Suśruta, namely the Sūtrasthāna, to be copied for the study of his sons and grandsons. May there be good fortune. It was copied by Rā(ula) Nārasiṃha of the Ābhyantara Nāgara community.

“I copied it as I saw it in the exemplar. Whether correct or incorrect, no blame should be assigned to me.”

Extent of the sections

Each colophon begins by recording the extent of the preceding section: 13,800 granthas for the Sūtrasthāna, 2,500 for the Nidānasthāna, and 2,800 for the Śārīrasthāna. Here grantha is a conventional unit of thirty-two syllables rather than a verse or physical line.

Date and historical setting

The three colophons give the same date for the commissioned copying of their respective sections: Vikrama Saṃvat 1525, the seventh tithi of the bright half of Bhādrapada, a Sunday. The weekday makes it possible to identify the date more precisely. Using M. Yano and M. Fushimi’s Pañcāṅga, I calculate the date as Sunday, 6 September 1467 in the Julian calendar, or 15 September 1467 in the proleptic Gregorian calendar. This calculation treats Vikrama Saṃvat 1525 as the current year, corresponding to 1524 elapsed years. It also follows Yano and Fushimi’s recommended procedure for handling the intercalary month (adhimāsa).

The place is given as Ahmedabad (Ahimadāvāda). The ruler is named as Sultan Śrī Maḥmūd, in whose “victorious reign” (vijayarājya) the copying took place. Given the date, this can be identified with Maḥmūd I Begaḍā, Sultan of Gujarat from 1458 to 1511.1

Commissioner and intended readers

The commissioner was the minister Śrī Māṇḍaṇa, son of the eminent physician and minister Śrī Nārāyaṇa. The copy was intended for the study of Māṇḍaṇa’s sons and grandsons. The colophon thus places its production within a learned family whose members combined medical knowledge with administrative service.

Māṇḍaṇa and his father belonged to the Nāgara Brahmin community, which was closely associated with the intellectual and administrative life of Gujarat. The colophons use the more specific designation Ābhyantara Nāgara. Its exact significance remains unclear, although the same community is mentioned in several other manuscript colophons.2

The scribe

The scribe belonged to the same Ābhyantara Nāgara community. In the colophon to the Śārīrasthāna, his name is clearly written as Rāula Nārasiṃha, with Rāula most probably forming part of the personal name. The corresponding akṣaras in the other two colophons are less clear. A more confident reading may become possible as we gain greater familiarity with the handwriting of the manuscript.

The familiar formula following the scribe’s name states that he copied the text as he found it in his exemplar and should not be blamed for either correct or incorrect readings. It thus places responsibility for any errors on the manuscript from which he copied.

Difficult readings

Several expressions remain problematic. The plural instrumental etaiḥ, placed after Māṇḍaṇa’s name, does not fit the expected Sanskrit construction, although its intended function is clear: Māṇḍaṇa is the person who caused the manuscript to be copied.

The designation of the work is also uncertain. The manuscript reads forms such as suśrutabhāṣyaṃ gayadāsāṣyaṃ. The second expression could reflect gayadāsasya, “of Gayadāsa,” or, more likely, a corrupt gayadāsākhyaṃ, “called Gayadāsa.” The translation above therefore uses the neutral formulation “Gayadāsa’s commentary on Suśruta” without adopting either emendation.

RORI 6838 and RORI 5157

The colophons also allow us to identify RORI 6838 with RORI 5157, now held at the Rajasthan Oriental Research Institute in Bikaner. RORI 5157 transmits Gayadāsa’s commentary on the Kalpasthāna. Its scribal colophon closely matches those of RORI 6838: both manuscripts name the same commissioner and give the same date and place of copying. The identification is further supported by their common layout and decoration. The two shelfmarks therefore represent different surviving parts of the same original manuscript.

Together, the two parts preserve the text from Sūtrasthāna 18 to the end of the Śārīrasthāna and the Kalpasthāna. The intervening Cikitsāsthāna and the subsequent Uttaratantra have not yet been located.

The Jaipur and Bikaner portions were probably once kept together as a single manuscript bundle. Their later separation, together with the loss of the Cikitsāsthāna and Uttaratantra, suggests that the manuscript may at some stage have been divided and handled in separate parts, perhaps to facilitate the study of individual sections. This remains a hypothesis, but it would help to explain the present distribution of its surviving portions.

entry.title: The Suśruta Project - 2025 Annual Report on Technical Infrastructure

link.title: The Suśruta Project - 2025 Annual Report on Technical Infrastructure

entry.content:
Prepared from the public record of the GitHub organization sushrutaproject1, the project website sushrutaproject1.github.io, Zenodo, and the INDOLOGY mailing list. Covers activity from January 1 to December 31, 2025. Compiled by Claude AI.

Overview

2025 was a transition year for the Suśruta Project. It marked the formal close of “The Suśruta Project 1.0” (2020–2024) — the SSHRC-funded study of the palm-leaf manuscript MS Kathmandu KL 699 (878 CE) and related witnesses of the Suśrutasaṃhitā — and the launch of its successor, “The Compendium of Suśruta in Time and Space: Mapping a Medical Tradition” (2025–2029). Both phases are led by Dominik Wujastyk (University of Alberta).

Major achievements

New five-year grant secured. SSHRC awarded Insight Grant 435-2025-0604, funding “Mapping a Medical Tradition” from 2025 through 2029, based at the University of Alberta. This is the project’s principal 2025 milestone: it converts the completed Phase 1 diplomatic transcription work into a funded program of critical editions, translations, and comparative study of the text’s transmission across South Asia, China, and Southeast Asia. The successor project maintains its own site and GitHub presence at sushrutaproject2.github.io.

Phase 1 edition brought to completion and re-archived. On May 15, 2025 the Sushrutasamhita_Saktumiva1 repository (the critical edition and its apparatus) reached release v.6.1, “Completed IIIF pointers for all witnesses” — every manuscript witness in the edition now links live to its IIIF facsimile images. A companion release on May 8, 2025 triggered Zenodo archiving of the repository for long-term preservation. Separately, an earlier edition state (v.4.3, the completed meta-editing of the Sūtrasthāna) was re-archived on Zenodo on April 9, 2025 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.15184815), noting eleven pull requests of translation and structural work behind that release.

Web infrastructure consolidated. In a message to the INDOLOGY list dated December 16, 2025, Wujastyk announced the reorganization of the project’s online presence: legacy content moved to sushrutaproject1.github.io (with a further simplification to sushrutaproject.github.io completed in early 2026), the old sushrutaproject.org domain now redirects to the new site, and the successor project’s material lives separately at sushrutaproject2.github.io. This tidied up several years of accumulated web infrastructure into a clear two-phase structure.

Continued editing and translation. Commit activity through the year shows steady, hands-on philological work rather than large batch imports: individual adhyāya (chapter) files were revised piece by piece — for example passages in Nidānasthāna, Cikitsāsthāna 4.4, and chapters such as 2.1, 3.1, 5.1, 5.8, and 6.65 — interspersed with translation-PDF regenerations, typo fixes, and footnotes (e.g., on the philosophical schools referenced in the text). A concentrated run of this work in early-to-mid December 2025 (at least 39 commits between December 4 and 22) followed what commit messages describe as project seminars and editing sessions. Collaborator Deepro Chakraborty contributed a cleanup of the Nidānasthāna text, merged via pull request #327 on December 20. Routine XML regeneration was handled by an automated “Wujastyk Bot” process rather than by hand.

Groundwork for a new presentation platform. A new repository, Sushrutasamhita_Saktumiva2, was created to present the same critical edition through “Saktumiva 2.0,” an updated version of the project’s custom manuscript-collation viewer — the beginning of a migration away from the original Saktumiva 1.0 interface.

Releases in 2025

Date Repository Tag Note

May 15, 2025 Sushrutasamhita_Saktumiva1 v.6.1 IIIF pointers completed for all manuscript witnesses
Apr 9, 2025 (Zenodo record date) Sushrutasamhita_Saktumiva1 v.4.3 Re-archived on Zenodo; 11 PRs of translation/structural work

Repositories active during the year

The sushrutaproject1 organization currently comprises five public repositories: Sushrutasamhita_Saktumiva1 (the main critical edition, TEI XML/TeX), the new Sushrutasamhita_Saktumiva2 (edition on the updated platform), sushrutaproject1.github.io (the project website), and a .github profile repository. All of the recorded 2025 activity above falls within the first two.

A note on the data

This report draws on what GitHub’s public pages and unauthenticated API allow without login credentials. Release, Zenodo, and mailing-list dates are exact. Commit figures, however, are drawn from spot samples (a full quarter and a three-week December window) rather than a complete year-long count, because GitHub’s unauthenticated API rate limit was reached repeatedly during research and search/date-filtered pages are blocked to automated fetches by GitHub’s own robots.txt. The one complete quarter that could be checked (April–June 2025) recorded 20 commits. Issue and pull-request history for 2025 could not be reliably retrieved for the same reason; PR #327 (merged December 20, 2025) is the one confirmed by name. A GitHub-authenticated review — for instance by connecting a personal access token, or by reviewing the repositories’ Insights pages directly in a browser — would allow a complete count.

Outlook

With Phase 1 archived and consolidated, 2026 activity is likely to concentrate on the newly funded Mapping a Medical Tradition project (sushrutaproject2) and on finishing the migration of the edition to the Saktumiva 2.0 platform.
